title: The Oak and the Reed
text:
On the bank of a river stood a great oak, with a trunk so thick that it had survived many winters. Near its roots grew a slender reed. The oak looked down on the reed with pity. The smallest breeze, it said, made the reed bow and tremble, while the oak stood firm and held its head high against the strongest winds.

The reed answered that it was not as frightened of the wind as the oak imagined. It bent, but it did not break.

That night a violent storm came down the valley. The wind roared and the rain lashed the trees. The reed bent low, almost to the water, and let the gusts pass over it. The oak refused to give way. It stood straight and resisted with all its strength.

The storm grew stronger still. At last, with a terrible crack, the oak was torn up by the roots and thrown down across the riverbank. When morning came and the wind died away, the reed straightened up again and stood exactly where it had stood before, beside the fallen giant.
lesson: Rigid strength can be the very thing that breaks you. In a crisis, the ability to bend, adapt and wait out the storm is often worth more than the will to stand firm.
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book I, Fable 22 (Le Chene et le Roseau), after Aesop
caveat: In Aesop's older version the oak is uprooted first and then asks the reeds how they survived; the conversation before the storm is La Fontaine's.
